## 2 Kings 5 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

The chapter records two of Elisha's miracles: the cleansing of Naaman the Syrian from leprosy (vv. 1–19) and the smiting of Gehazi with that same leprosy (vv. 20–27). Matthew Henry notes that our Lord Himself refers to this event in Luke 4:27, making Naaman's cure a type of the calling of the Gentiles. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_kings/5.htm)

---

### v. 1 — Naaman's Greatness and His Leprosy

**Traditional Reading:** Naaman ("pleasantness") was commander of the army of the king of Aram (Ben-Hadad II). He was a "great man" and "highly respected" — the Hebrew idiom literally means "lifted up of face," indicating special favour (Ellicott). The striking theological note is that "by him the LORD had given victory to Aram" — it is Jehovah, not the Syrian gods Hadad or Rimmon, who grants victory even to pagan nations. This asserts God's absolute sovereignty over international affairs (Precept Austin). Gill adds the Jewish tradition that Naaman was the man who "drew the bow at a venture" that killed Ahab (1 Kings 22:34). Yet all his glory is undercut by the devastating "but he was a leper." The Hebrew *tsara* covers a range of skin diseases, not necessarily Hansen's disease (Precept Austin notes Dale Ralph Davis says Hansen's lesions are never white, yet Gehazi later becomes "white as snow"). Even if the condition did not incapacitate him, it rendered him ritually unclean by Israelite standards and was socially stigmatising.

### vv. 2–3 — The Testimony of the Servant Girl

**Traditional Reading:** A young Israelite girl, taken captive in a Syrian raid, serves Naaman's wife. She says, "If only my master would go to the prophet who is in Samaria, he would cure him of his leprosy." Guzik calls her "an unwilling missionary" — her tragedy became the instrument of salvation. Clarke (cited by Guzik) notes: "See the benefits of a religious education! Had not this little maid been brought up in the knowledge of the true God, she had not been the instrument of so great a salvation." The Pulpit Commentary homily stresses she "did not forget her religion when she went from home." Her faith was simple but bold: she spoke up, she believed Elisha could heal, and she cared enough to say so.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-5/

### vv. 4–5 — Naaman and the King of Aram Respond

**Traditional Reading:** Naaman reports the girl's words to his master, the king of Aram (Ben-Hadad II). The king sends Naaman with a letter to the king of Israel and lavish gifts: ten talents of silver, six thousand shekels of gold, and ten sets of clothing. Ellicott estimates the silver at about £3,750 and the gold at about £13,500 in Victorian currency, though he suspects the numbers may be textually corrupt. Guzik estimates over $1.2 million in modern value, illustrating Naaman's desperation. The gifts also reflect ancient Near Eastern diplomatic custom — one approached a foreign power with costly presents.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-5/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/5.htm

### vv. 6–7 — The Letter and the King of Israel's Panic

**Traditional Reading:** The letter from the king of Aram simply says: "I am sending my servant Naaman, so that you may cure him of his leprosy." The king of Israel (Jehoram, son of Ahab) tears his clothes in distress — an act associated with hearing blasphemy (Ellicott; cf. Matthew 26:65). He cries, "Am I God, killing and giving life?" — alluding to Deuteronomy 32:39 and 1 Samuel 2:6, where only Yahweh holds power over life and death. Leprosy was considered a "living death" (Numbers 12:12). Jehoram assumes the Syrian king is "seeking a quarrel" — a pretext for war. Guzik notes that the Syrian king wrongly assumed Jehoram had a good relationship with Elisha: "It is easy for others to assume that we have a better relationship with God than we really do."

### vv. 8–9 — Elisha Intervenes

**Traditional Reading:** Elisha hears of the king's distress and sends a message: "Why have you torn your clothes? Please let the man come to me, and he will know that there is a prophet in Israel." This is a gentle rebuke to Jehoram — his panic is needless. Ellicott notes that Jehoram did not think of Elisha because king and prophet were not on good terms (cf. 2 Kings 3:14). Naaman arrives with impressive horses and chariots and stands at the door of Elisha's house. The "standing at the door" may reflect ancient protocol: those consulting a great prophet did not presume to enter (Ellicott, citing Keil), or, as Bähr suggests, Elisha's house was a "poor hovel" the great man would not deign to enter.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-5/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/5.htm

### vv. 10–12 — The Simple Command and Naaman's Rage

**Traditional Reading:** Elisha does not even come out to Naaman but sends a messenger: "Go and wash yourself seven times in the Jordan, and your flesh will be restored, and you will be clean." Ellicott notes two reasons: (1) Elisha avoided personal contact with a leper; (2) the command makes clear the healing comes from God, not any magical gesture by the prophet. Guzik stresses this was humbling for Naaman, who expected an elaborate prophetic ceremony: Elisha coming out, standing, calling on God's name, and waving his hand over the spot (v. 11). Naaman's rage reveals he had "anticipated a way God would work, and he was offended when God didn't work the way he expected." He names the Abanah (or Amana) and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, as superior to Israel's muddy Jordan. Ellicott identifies these as the present-day Barada and Nahr el-Awaj, both clear mountain streams.

Spurgeon (cited by Guzik and Precept Austin) identifies two enemies Naaman fought: "Proud Self" (who demanded special treatment) and "Evil Questioning" (who questioned why the Jordan). The College Press series labels this whole section (vv. 8–14) "Naaman's Cleansing."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-5/

### v. 13 — The Wise Counsel of Naaman's Servants

**Traditional Reading:** Naaman's servants approach him respectfully ("My father") and use brilliant logic: "If the prophet had told you to do some great thing, would you not have done it? How much more, then, when he tells you, 'Wash and be cleansed'?" Guzik observes: if Elisha had asked Naaman to sacrifice 100 or 1,000 animals, he would have done it immediately; the command was refused because it was easy and humbling. This is a recurring spiritual principle: God's simple commands often prove the hardest to obey because they strip away human pride.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-5/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/5.htm

### v. 14 — Naaman Is Healed

**Traditional Reading:** Naaman "went down" (from Samaria to the Jordan valley — Ellicott) and dipped seven times "according to the word of the man of God." Each dip was a step of faith. Guzik cites Spurgeon: Naaman overcame Proud Self and Evil Questioning to achieve total obedience. JFB notes that seven was "the symbol of the covenant" (Keil) — the cure rested on God's covenant with Israel. The result: "his flesh was restored like that of a little child, and he was clean." Guzik notes that the simple method, done without the prophet present, "gave God the credit" — the healing was obviously from Yahweh, not magical incantation.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-5/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/2-kings-5.html

### vv. 15–16 — Naaman's Confession and Elisha's Refusal

**Traditional Reading:** Naaman returns with his entire company, now entering Elisha's house (contrast v. 9). His confession is remarkable: "Now I know for sure that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel." Ellicott notes the "mark of historic truth": Naaman still thinks in local-deity terms ("no God in all the earth except in Israel"), yet this is genuine monotheistic confession for a Gentile. He offers a "blessing" (a gift — Genesis 33:11), but Elisha steadfastly refuses, swearing "As surely as the LORD lives, before whom I stand, I will not accept it." JFB explains that Elisha wanted the Syrians to see that God's servants act from piety, not mercenary motives, contrasting sharply with heathen priests and prophets. Guzik: "some acts of ministry must be kept free from financial entanglement to give God the credit and guard the prophet's integrity."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-5/

### vv. 17–18 — Naaman's Two Requests: Earth and Rimmon

**Traditional Reading:** Naaman makes two requests:

**(1) Two mule-loads of earth (v. 17):** Guzik calls this "superstitious" — Naaman held the common ancient view that deities had power over particular places. He wanted Israelite soil to build an altar to Yahweh in Syria (cf. Exodus 20:24). Patterson and Austel (cited by Guzik) suggest the soil was "a tangible reminder of his cleansing and new relationship to God."

**(2) Bowing in the temple of Rimmon (v. 18):** As the king's right-hand man ("leans on my arm" is a metaphor for chief attendant — Ellicott, Wiseman), Naaman was expected to accompany his master into the temple of the Syrian storm-god Rimmon (Assyrian Rammânu, "the thunderer" — Ellicott). He asks that the LORD pardon him when he must bow there.

Elisha's response ("Go in peace," v. 19a) is deliberately non-specific. Guzik says Elisha "left the matter up to Naaman and God," trusting that the LORD would personally convict Naaman about idolatry.

**Translation Debate (Clarke, Trapp, Lightfoot, Gill):** Some older commentators argue Naaman is confessing *past* idolatry, not asking permission for future acts. The Hebrew can be read this way: "When my master went into the house of Rimmon… and I worshipped there… the LORD pardon your servant." Gill and Lightfoot favour this reading, making Naaman a true penitent. However, Ellicott and most modern commentators take it as a request about future unavoidable participation. Haydock (Catholic) notes that Josephus "passes over this history… unless he was staggered at the petition of Naaman" (v. 18).

### vv. 19b–20 — Gehazi's Greed Awakens

**Traditional Reading:** After Naaman departs "a short distance" (Hebrew *kibrāh* of ground — an unspecified but short distance, not a parasang, Ellicott), Gehazi, Elisha's servant, resolves to run after him. His inner monologue reveals his heart: "My master has spared this Aramean" — Gehazi considers Naaman an enemy alien who should have been "spoiled." Guzik notes that Gehazi became "exactly what Elisha avoided: becoming a taker." Gill says Gehazi's real grievance was that *he* got no share.

### vv. 21–24 — Gehazi's Deception and Naaman's Generosity

**Traditional Reading:** Naaman sees Gehazi running and, in a mark of great respect, "got down from the chariot to meet him" (literally "fell from off the chariot" — an expression of haste, Ellicott). He asks, "Is everything all right?" Gehazi lies: two young prophets have arrived from Ephraim, and Elisha now requests a talent of silver and two sets of clothing. Ellicott calls this "a downright lie" and "highly improbable" — had Naaman reflected, he might have seen through it, but his heart was "so filled with gratitude" that he was glad to give. Naaman generously urges him to take *two* talents, ties them in bags with clothing, and has two of his own servants carry them (a courteous touch — Ellicott). Gehazi stashes the goods at "the hill" (Hebrew *'ōphel*, a mound or fortified hill, perhaps part of Samaria's defences — Ellicott) and dismisses Naaman's men.

### vv. 25–27 — Gehazi Exposed, Judged, and Leprous

**Traditional Reading:** Gehazi presents himself before Elisha, who asks, "Where have you been?" Gehazi lies: "Your servant did not go anywhere." Elisha then reveals his supernatural knowledge: "Did not my spirit go with you when the man got down from his chariot to meet you?" (Ellicott renders it: "Nor did my heart go away when a man turned from his chariot to meet thee" — a severe irony adopting Gehazi's own phrase). The Targum paraphrases: "By the spirit of prophecy I was informed."

Elisha's question, "Is this the time to accept money and clothing, olive groves and vineyards, sheep and oxen, menservants and maidservants?" reveals the covetous heart behind the act: Gehazi didn't bring all this home, but these were the things he *wanted* (Guzik, citing G. Campbell Morgan). Morgan adds: "The deepest wrong… was that it involved the Divine witness which had been borne to the Syrian… by the little serving maid… and the prophet Elisha. Their actions had been wholly disinterested, and for the glory of God."

The judgment: "The leprosy of Naaman will cling to you and your descendants forever." Gehazi leaves "leprous — as white as snow." JFB (citing Keil) says the punishment was not too severe: it was not covetousness alone, but "the ill use made of the prophet's name to gain an object prompted by a mean covetousness, and the attempt to conceal it by lying." Ellicott notes that leprosy is hereditary, so the curse on descendants is medically realistic. Dilday (cited by Guzik) summarises: "a pagan healed by faith, an Israelite cursed by dishonor." Guzik adds: "God allowed him to keep the riches, but also gave him the other thing Naaman had — severe leprosy."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-5/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/5.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/2-kings-5.html

## Distinctive Protestant Traditions

### Reformed / Presbyterian

The Reformed reading (visible in JFB/Keil, and Precept Austin's compilations) emphasises **divine sovereignty**. The key theological point in v. 1 is that *Yahweh*, not Syrian gods, gave victory to Aram — God governs all nations, not just Israel. Precept Austin calls this the "Paradoxical Principle of 100% Dependent and 100% Responsible." The healing through the Jordan's waters is tied to God's *covenant* with Israel (Keil: seven dips because seven is "the signature of the works of God" and the symbol of the covenant). The refusal of payment (v. 16) underscores that grace is free and cannot be purchased — a Reformation emphasis. The judgment on Gehazi is seen as a just exercise of covenant curse for profaning God's name.

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-5-commentary
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/2-kings-5.html

### Baptist (Spurgeon / Gill)

Spurgeon's sermon "The Rule of Grace" (referenced by both Guzik and StudyLight) treats Naaman's healing as illustrating both **the sovereignty of divine grace** (Naaman was a Gentile, many Israelite lepers were not healed — Luke 4:27) and **the unvarying rules by which that grace works**: hearing the message (the little maid), obeying the command (wash), and being humbled first. Spurgeon stresses that "there is no sinner, be the purposes of God what they may, who will ever get his sins forgiven except by washing in the precious blood of Jesus." Gill, the classic Baptist commentator, identifies Naaman's request about Rimmon as confession of *past* idolatry, making him a genuine proselyte ("proselyte of righteousness").

- https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-rule-of-grace
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-5.html

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)

The Pentecostal/charismatic emphasis, while fully orthodox, highlights the **miraculous and the practical dynamics of faith**. Guzik stresses that each dip was "a step of faith," that Naaman had to fight off internal enemies (Spurgeon's Proud Self and Evil Questioning), and that God works through simple, humbling obedience rather than elaborate displays. There is also emphasis on the **prophetic gift**: Elisha's spirit went with Gehazi (v. 26) — whether supernatural knowledge or observation, Guzik leaves open, but the charismatic reading tends toward a genuine word of knowledge. The testimony of the servant girl is held up as a model for Spirit-led witness in difficult circumstances.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-5/

### Reformed Baptist / Desiring God (John Piper)

In a sermon referencing 2 Kings 5, Piper draws a parallel between Gehazi and the rich young ruler. He emphasises that Naaman "didn't just lose leprosy. He lost pride. He lost false religion." Grace humbled him. Piper's application focuses on the danger of greed in ministry, echoing Elisha's refusal to "peddle God." Elisha's question — "Is it a time to receive money…?" — is treated as a warning against those who turn ministry into a means of personal gain.

- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/remember-the-rich-young-man

### Anglican (Ellicott)

Ellicott, writing for English readers of the established Church, provides the most detailed historical, linguistic, and archaeological notes. He identifies Rimmon with the Assyrian Rammânu ("the thunderer"), notes the parallel in Assyrian exorcism texts where bathing in sacred waters is prescribed, and discusses textual variants. His tone is scholarly and restrained, and he treats Naaman's request about Rimmon as a sincere but imperfect request for accommodation, which Elisha grants with "Go in peace."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/5.htm

## Catholic Reading (Haydock)

The Haydock Catholic Commentary notes that Josephus "passes over this history. It is not known for what reason, unless he was staggered at the petition of Naaman, ver. 18, 19" — suggesting the Rimmon incident was seen as theologically awkward. The Catholic NRSV-CE renders "leper" as "suffered from leprosy" (v. 1). Haydock also notes the Rabbinical tradition that Naaman killed Ahab. Beyond these brief notes, the Catholic reading does not diverge substantially from the traditional Protestant interpretation of the chapter; the emphasis falls on the universality of God's saving mercy (a Gentile is healed while many in Israel are not — prefiguring the Church's mission to the nations).

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/2_kings/5.htm

## Modern Scholarship Notes

Precept Austin cites the ESV Study Bible's observation that Naaman's "leprosy" (Hebrew *metsora*) was "some kind of disfigurement of the skin (but not necessarily what is known by modern people as 'leprosy')." Dale Ralph Davis (2 Kings, cited by Precept Austin) argues Naaman's condition "was not necessarily Hansen's disease" but "may have been some form of psoriasis or scabies or other skin disease," since Gehazi's lesions were "as white as snow" and Hansen's disease lesions "are never white." Ellicott notes a striking ancient Near Eastern parallel: among Assyrian exorcism texts from before 2200 B.C., the god Hea instructs a sick man to bathe in the sacred waters at the mouth of the Euphrates — indicating that Elisha's command "acted in accordance with ancient Semitic belief as to the healing virtue of running streams."

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-5-commentary
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/5.htm

## Key Themes (Across Traditions)

1. **God's sovereignty over all nations** — Yahweh gives victory even to pagans (v. 1).
2. **Salvation for the Gentiles** — Naaman prefigures the inclusion of Gentiles (Luke 4:27).
3. **The simplicity and humbling nature of faith** — washing in the Jordan required no great deed, only obedient trust.
4. **Grace cannot be bought** — Elisha refuses payment; God's gifts are free.
5. **The danger of greed and hypocrisy in ministry** — Gehazi's judgment is severe because he corrupted a pure witness.
6. **God uses the lowly** — a captive slave girl becomes the channel of salvation for a mighty general.
